cards.explanation: The answer is False. Hiram, king of Tyre, was no enemy of David, Solomon's father. The verse says “…Hiram had always been a friend of David.” (1 Kings 5:1) Hiram sends envoys to Solomon, the new king, and that friendship is part of the story from the very first verse.

The answer is wars. Solomon, Israel's king, tells Hiram that his father David “…could not build a house for the Name of the LORD his God until the LORD had put his enemies under his feet.” (1 Kings 5:3) The wars were waged on all sides against David. I think a man with that many fronts open barely had time to sit down, never mind build.

The answer is that David's son would build it. Solomon, Israel's king, quotes what the LORD told his father David: “I will put your son on your throne in your place, and he will build the house for My Name.” (1 Kings 5:5) So Solomon isn't just making a plan on his own. He says he's building according to what the LORD said.

The reason Solomon gives is that nobody in Israel logs like the Sidonians. Solomon, Israel's king, tells Hiram, king of Tyre, “…you know that there are none among us as skilled in logging as the Sidonians.” (1 Kings 5:6) He's saying Hiram's people are the ones for the job. He even offers to pay whatever wages Hiram sets.

The answer is True, and Hiram says it out loud. Hiram, king of Tyre, receives the message from Solomon, Israel's king, and says, “Blessed be the LORD this day! He has given David a wise son over this great people!” (1 Kings 5:7) The text says he rejoiced greatly. The first thing out of his mouth is praise to the LORD.

The answer is that he floats them as rafts by sea. Hiram, king of Tyre, says, “My servants will haul the logs from Lebanon to the Sea, and I will float them as rafts by sea to the place you specify.” (1 Kings 5:9) Logs on the water, riding along to wherever Solomon, Israel's king, names. I've never had anything that big ride on water, and I'd sink if I tried.

The answer is False, friends. Hiram, king of Tyre, says to Solomon, Israel's king, “And in exchange, you can meet my needs by providing my household with food.” (1 Kings 5:9) Free timber? Not from this king. He wants a trade, and he names it right up front: food for his household. Me, I would have asked for cookies, but nobody consults the stamper.

The answer is False. The verse says “…year after year Solomon would provide Hiram with 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, as well as 20,000 baths of pure olive oil.” (1 Kings 5:11) Solomon, Israel's king, keeps sending it to Hiram, king of Tyre. It happens year after year, not once.

The answer is True. The text says, “And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised him.” (1 Kings 5:12) Solomon is Israel's king, and the words “…as He had promised him.” tell us the LORD made that promise first. Then He kept it.

The answer is that there was peace and they made a treaty. The verse says, “There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.” (1 Kings 5:12) Hiram is king of Tyre and Solomon is Israel's king, so this is an official agreement between two kings. Peace and a treaty, both in one verse.

The answer is two months. Solomon, Israel's king, sent the workers “…in monthly shifts of 10,000 men, so that they would spend one month in Lebanon and two months at home.” (1 Kings 5:14) One month away, two months back home. I think those men were glad to see their own front doors.

The answer is large costly dressed stones. The text says the king commanded them “…to quarry large, costly stones to lay the foundation of the temple with dressed stones.” (1 Kings 5:17) That king is Solomon, Israel's king. Dressed stones are stones that have been cut and shaped, so these aren't raw rocks pulled straight from the ground. Large, costly and dressed, all in one order.

The answer is False. The verse says, “So Solomon’s and Hiram’s builders, along with the Gebalites, quarried the stone and prepared the timber and stone for the construction of the temple.” (1 Kings 5:18) Solomon is Israel's king, and Hiram is king of Tyre, so builders from both kingdoms are on the job. The Gebalites are named too. And friends, this story isn't over.
